Testimony of Adam Goode, Maine AFL-CIO Legislative & Political Director, In Opposition to LD 618,
"An Act to Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until 9 p.m. During the School Year and Until 10 p.m. During Summer Vacation" and LD 644, "An Act to Expand Employment Opportunities for
Minor Students by Eliminating Certain Work Limitations"

Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Labor, my name is Adam Goode. I'm the Legislative and Political Director of the Maine AFL~CIO. We represent 40,000 working people in the state of Maine. We work to improve the lives and working conditions of our members and all
working people. We testify in opposition to LD 618 and LD 644.
Current law states that young people who are 14 and 15 years old can work until 7 PM during the school year and until 9 PM during summer vacation. LD 618 would allow 14 and 15 year olds to work until 9 PM during the school year and until 10 PM during summer vacation.

LD 644 repeals the child labor laws for young people who are 16 and 17 years old. These include a repeal of the
laws that say a 16 or 17 year old cannot work more than 24 hours a week when school is in session, more than 6 hours a day when school is in session and more than 50 hours a week and 10 hours a day when school is not in session. It repeals the law that says children cannot work more than 6 consecutive days. It also repeals the law
saying children cannot work after 10:15 PM or before 7 AM on school days and aiter midnight and before 5 AM on non school days. It repeals the law that says children under 17 cannot work when school is in session
and eliminates all record keeping rules for child labor.

Most importantly, it does not replace these guardrails with any law to govern hours that 16 and 17 year olds work, which would be a serious departure from Maine's history of recognizing the importance of young people focusing on educational achievement and the unique workplace safety issues that arise from young people

performing Work tasks that are often designed for adults.

i

These bills are a departure from our child labor laws that were enacted back in 1991. The Maine AFL-C10, the Girl Scouts and others were leading advocates for those positive changes.

Maine legislators began drafting labor law in the middle of the 19*` century. Child labor was one of their first areas of concern. From the outset, our labor law prioritized educational achievement over work for children and teens. Our first child labor law passed in 1847 and it made educational requirements in order to work. This bill
nins afoul of Maine's tradition of passing laws that emphasize the importance of education over work.

Printed In House with Union Labor

The 1991 laws were spurred on by a number of events happening in Maine at the time. One was the death of a 15 year old who was working illegally on a trash truck. Another was a stream of complaints from the educational community regarding students falling asleep in class due to late hours of work. At that time Maine
had one of the highest truancy and dropout rates in the nation. Addressing truancy and workplace safety are major motivations for having strong child workplace laws.
Attempts to weaken Maine's child labor laws by allowing students to work more hours even when school is in session will take us backwards on workplace safety. Young people are injured on the job more than others,
partially due to inexperience, partially due to improper training and paitially due to being expected to use equipment designed for adults. Longer hours in the workplace for children will lead to more injuries.
Our current statute allows young people to work while encouraging young people to gain the strongest education possible. The current law says those aged 16 and 17 can work up to 24 hours a week when school is
in session, including until 10:15 pm on school nights. This allows for instilling a work ethic in young people
while building a strong educational foundation.
Finally, we would remind the committee that education and schooling instills work ethic in children. A l6 year
old has their entire life ahead of them to work more than 24 hours a week or after 10:15 pm. The Window of life when a child can take full advantage of the skills related to work ethic learned in schools is limited and should
be taken full advantage of.

MEA OPPOSITION TO LD 112, 618, and 644
Dear Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and members of the Committee:
My name is Ben Grant and l am the General Counsel of the Maine Education Association. The MEA
is a labor union representing about 24,000 educators and support staff in nearly every public
school in the state, in both the University of Maine and Community College systems, and in several Academy schools. In addition, thousands of retired educators continue their advocacy work through the MEA-Retired program. The MEA, and the labor movement as a whole, has a long history
of advocating for sensible labor laws in Maine, and personally I have represented hundreds of
working people in Maine in various kinds of legal actions. In addition, the MEA has long advocated for reasonable laws regarding children and minors, given our members' first-hand experience in the
classroom.
Forthat reason, the MEA opposes LD 112,618, and 644, and urges the Committee to vote ought not
to pass.
LD 112: While there may not be a direct correlation to wage rates and success in the classroom, it must be noted that sub-minimum wages for minors has a long and scandalous history in this
country. The simple fact is that making this change invites abuse and exploitation of children. it
may be that there is a benevolent intent in this proposal, but the history of industrial relations virtually guarantees that some employers will not be able to resist the lure of low wages to both undercut the adult workforce and to overwork youth who need to be focused on other things.
LD 618 & 644: These proposals should be defeated because they erode the proper balance between work, education, and "being a kid." There can be no serious argument that students can best engage in their education when they are rested and ready. These bills peel away several protections in Maine law designed to ensure that is happening on a daily basis. Simply put: more than 6 hours of work on a school day is too much. For students who are still minors, our policy
needs to be directed at the fulfillment and betterment of their education. We still allow ample time
for employment, but at that age time spent in and on education is more important- and our policy
should reflect that value.
Thank you, and the MEA urges a No vote on all of these bills.

Testimony of Chrissy Kimball
LD 618, An Act to Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until 9 p.m.
During the School Year and Until 10 p.m. During Summer Vacation
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Labor March 17, 2025
Testimony in Support of LD 618
Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and esteemed members of the Committee on Labor,
my name is Chrissy Kimball, and I am the owner of The Log Yard Dairy Bar in Poland. I am here
today to testify in favor of LD 618.
Three years ago, I opened the windows of my frozen custard shop for the first time. I rounded up a few local teenagers I already knew, and we dove in headfirst. By our second year, I had teenagers banging on my door, eager for a job.
We often hear people say, "Kids these days are lazy. They can't problem-solve. They're just glued to video games." It is NOT that our kids are inherently bums- It is that our safety
obsessed culture keeps these teens in the basement on their screens where they are safe and
sound. In my opinion, that's the most dangerous place for them.
Last spring, I interviewed over 40 teenagers forjust a handful of positions. I eventually had to stop accepting applications. The most ambitious of the bunch? The 14- and 15-year-olds. They are eager. They are bored. They want to do something meaningful, something they choose for themselves, something that gives them a sense of independence.

Yet, many of my fellow business owners won't hire this age group because of the restrictions
placed on them by the government---restrictions that assume the state knows what's best for
our kids.
14 and 15 year olds START their soccer games at 7pm. Some kids return home from away games at 10pm! And this is tax payer funded! Every day, we glorify ath|etes--the quarterback, the star player. I have three children. One is an athlete. Another would have started working as a logger at age three if I had let him. One path is not more noble than the other. Yet tonight, my 9-year-old son will be at REC baseball practice from 7 to 8:30 p.m., while the 14-year-old who
wants to work is forced to go home.
What message are we sending? That recreation is always the priority? Theatre, music, and
sports all take place after 7 p.m., but work is restricted? We have an opportunity with this bill to
encourage a strong work ethic among the kids who want or need to work. Right now, many 14and 15-year-olds struggle to find jobs--not because they lack the ability or motivation, but
because the law stands in their way.
There's a harmful narrative that employers are the enemy---exploiters looking to take advantage
of young workers. But we need to flip that mindset. Employers provide opportunities. They take
risks. They serve as mentors, guiding young people as they learn responsibility, problem-solving, and real-world skills.
l am here in support of this bill--not for myself. l could easily hire 16- and 17-year-olds and avoid the restrictions altogether. l am here for:
� The 14-year-old who wants to take driver's ed and has to save up to pay for it himself. 0 The 15-year-old who isn't into sports and would otherwise be drowning in video games. 0 The kid who wants to start an IRA at age 14 and get ahead in life.

These kids are capable. They are eager. They are ready to learn. lt's time for the state to step aside and let them. Thank you for your time and consideration. l would be happy to answer any questions.

RE: Testimony in SUPPORT of LD 618: An Act to Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until 9 p.m. During the School Year and Until 10 p.m. During Summer Vacation:
Dear Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder and members of the Labor Committee:
The Maine Grocers & Food Producers Association and the Retail Association of Maine are providing joint
testimony in support of LD 618: An Act to Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until 9 p.m. During the School Year and Until 10 p.m. During Summer Vacation. Our business trade associations represent Main Street businesses including independently owned and operated grocery stores and supermarkets, general
merchandise and specialty retailers, convenience stores, distributors, and supporting partners -- together
representing more than 450 members statewide. Maine's retail sector employs more than 85,000 Mainers.
This bill represents a reasonable modernization of Maine's child labor laws, aligning our state with national norms while preserving safeguards for young workers.
Currently, Maine restricts work for minors under 16 to end by 7 p.m. during the school year. By contrast, 14 states allow minors under 16 to work until at least 9 p.m. during the school year. These states include:
Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Montana, New Hampshire, North Dakota,
Oregon, South Dakota, Washington, and Wisconsin.
Notably, New Hampshire allows minors to work until 9 p.m. during the school year, and there have been no documented issues or harms resulting from this policy. Despite New Hampshire's more flexible law, there are
no widespread reports of negative outcomes tied to minors working until 9 p.m., such as academic decline or
health risks.
While I recognize the importance of balancing work and education for youth, extending allowable work hours modestly by two hours in the evening provides families and businesses with greater flexibility. This change

could support small businesses---especially in hospitality and retail sectors---that rely on part-time youth labor, while giving young people more opportunities to earn and learn workplace skills.

If the committee is hesitant to make a change, we would encourage the Committee to consider an amendment adding a sunset clause--perhaps two or three years----and require the Maine Department of
Labor to report back on the impacts of this law change. This measured approach allows the state to evaluate whether any unintended consequences emerge and take action if needed.

l respectfully urge you to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 618.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Testimony of Rep. David Boyer introducing
LD 618, An Act to Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until 9 p.m. During the
School Year and Until 10 p.m. During Summer Vacation
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Labor
March 18, 2025
Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder and esteemed members of the Committee on Labor, my name is Rep. David Boyer and I am proud to present LD 618, An Act to Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until
9 p.m. During the School Year and Until 10 p.m. During Summer Vacation. This bill does exactly what the title
says and amends the hours minors under 16 years of age can work.
This legislation offers a valuable opportunity to empower young people with work experience, financial
independence, and a stronger connection to their communities, while supporting businesses and the economy.
Allowing minors under 16 to work until 9 p.m. during the school year and 10 p.m. during summer vacation provides them with critical opportunities to gain practical skills like responsibility, time management, and teamwork---skills that prepare them for future success. For many, working is also a way to contribute to family
income or save for college, especially in low-income households. Businesses, particularly in retail and hospitality, would benefit from a larger pool of workers for evening shifts, addressing labor shortages and strengthening local economies.
While concerns about education, safety, and federal compliance are valid, they can be addressed with sensible safeguards. Compliance with federal law can be achieved by focusing on low-risk jobs and seeking exemptions where necessary. Illinois already allows similar exceptions for park district activities, proving that such measures can work. Additionally, there is legislation from Sen. Daughtry that would require schools to begin no later 8:30 a.m. which could help address concerns about students getting a full night of sleep.
In conclusion, this bill balances opportunity with responsibility. It allows minors to gain experience, eam
income, and support their communities, while ensuring their education and safety remain priorities. I urge the committee to support this legislation and invest in the future of our young people. Thank you for your time and
consideration.

To the Joint Standing Committee on Labor

Hearing, March 18, 2025

Good afternoon Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on_Labor. My name is Dillon Murray, Legislative Liaison for the Maine Department of Labor (Department). I am here today to speak on behalf of the Department in opposition to LD
618, "An Act to Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until 9 p.m. During the School Year and Until 10 p.m. During Summer Vacation."

The Maine Department of Labor is committed to connecting young people with opportunities for meaningful work experience. There is great value in obtaining a work permit as a minor, learning essential job skills, and gaining valuable workplace experience. Employment opportunities must be balanced with the need for school-based learning and the overall well--being of young workers. School remains the primary responsibility of minors, and labor laws have been carefully designed to ensure that work does not negatively impact education, health, and safety.

Maine Law (Maine Department of Labor)
Under current Maine law, minors under 16 years of age:
- May not work later than 7 p.m. during the school year. o May not work later than 9 p.m. during the summer months (June 1 through Labor
Day).

Federal Law (Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Part 570) The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) sets restrictions on the employment of minors under 16,
which include:
- During the school year: No work past 7 p.m. - During non-school weeks (June 1 through Labor Day): No work past 9 p.m.

Because LD 618 proposes extending work hours beyond federal limitations, the bill would be in
conflict with federal law, meaning that if enacted, Maine employers who allowed minors to work past 7 pm during the school year or 9 pm in the summer would be in violation of Federal
statute.
Child labor laws exist to protect the health, education, and safety of minors. Historically, these laws were established in response to exploitative labor practices that harmed children's physical and mental well-being. Studies have consistently shown that excessive work hours for minors can lead to:
- Academic decline -- Late work hours negatively impact school performance and increase
dropout rates.
- Increased fatigue and stress -- Sleep deprivation due to late shifts affects cognitive function and mental health.
- Higher workplace injury rates -- Younger workers, particularly in industries such as food sen/ice and retail, are at greater risk of workplace accidents due to inexperience and
fatigue.
While the Department supports employment opportunities for minors, we respectfully oppose
LD 618 due to its conflict with federal law and the potential negative impacts on young workers'
education, health, and safety. However, we recognize that policy decisions rest with this
Committee. Should any changes be made, MDOL stands ready to implement them and educate
both employers and workers on any updates to labor laws.
Thank you for your time and attention. l would be happy to answer any questions you may have
l
now or at a future work session.
The Maine Department of Labor is committed to serving Maine workers and businesses by helping employers recruit and train a talented workforce, providing workers with skills needed to compete in our economy, assisting individuals when jobs are lost, aiding people with disabilities reach career goals, ensuring safe and fair workplaces for people on thejob and providing research and analysis of employment data to supportjob growth.

Testimony of Jake Lachance
Government Relations Specialist
Maine State Chamber of Commerce
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Labor
In Support to
LD 112 "An Act to Promote Opportunities by Establishing a Student Wage",
LD 618 "An Act to Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until 9 p.m. During the School Year and Until 10 p.m. During Summer Vacation",
LD 644 "An Act to Expand Employment Opportunities for Minor Students by Eliminating Certain Work Limitations
Sen. Tipping, Rep. Roeder, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Labor, my name is Jake Lachance, and I am a Government Relations Specialist for the Maine State Chamber of Commerce, which advocates for over 5,000 large and small businesses across the State of Maine. I am honored to
provide testimony in support of Legislative Documents 112, 618, and 644, each of which serves to enhance employment opportunities for young individuals in Maine. Collectively, these bills strike a balance between fostering workforce participation, promoting economic growth, and maintaining
reasonable safeguards for student workers.
Support for LD 112: An Act to Promote Opportunities by Establishing a Student Wage LD 112 introduces a minimum wage structure specifically for secondary school students, allowing them to earn 50% ofthe state's minimum wage for a period of two years or until graduation. This measure acknowledges the unique employment status of students who seek to gain work
experience while balancing academic responsibilities. By offering a lower entry-level wage, businesses are more likely to hire and train students, providing invaluable workforce exposure that equips them
with lifelong skills. This bill encourages job creation and economic participation among youth while maintaining fairness in wage structures. As a result, we would anticipate that more employers would offer employment for secondary school students, invest the training and career development into these
individuals, and ultimately expand career opportunities for secondary school students.
Support for LD 618: An Act to Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until 9 p.m. During the School Year and Until 10 p.m. During Summer Vacation
LD 618 extends working hours for minors under 16 years old, permitting them to work until 9 p.m. during the academic year and 10 p.m. in the summer. This proposal reflects the modern realities of the workforce, where flexibility is key. Many industries, particularly retail and hospitality, require evening workers, and this bill allows young employees to contribute effectively while still prioritizing their education. With parental oversight and continued compliance with federal labor regulations, this bill provides an opportunity for youth to develop responsibility and financial independence.

Testimony of Nate Cloutier
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Labor l\/larch 18, 2025
In Support of LD 618, "An Act Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until 9 p.m. During the School Year and Until 10 p.m. During Summer Vacation"
Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Labor, my name is Nate Cloutier, and l am here today on behalf of HospitalityMaine, representing I\/laine's restaurant and lodging industries. I am also testifying on behalf of the Maine Tourism Association (MTA).
MTA has been promoting Maine and supporting members in every type of tourism business, such as
lodging, restaurants, camps, campgrounds, retail, guides, tour operators, amusements, and historical and cultural attractions for over 100 years. Hospitalitylvlaine and the Maine Tourism Association support LD 618, "An Act Allow Minors Under 16 Years of Age to Work Until 9 p.m. During the School Year and Until 10
p.m. During Summer Vacation."
LD 618 would allow minors under 16 years of age to work until 9 p.m. during the school year and until 10
p.m. during summer vacation.
Maine's hospitality and tourism sectors are vital components of our state's economy, attracting millions
of visitors annually. In 2023, Maine welcomed approximately 15.3 million visitors who contributed over $9 billion in direct spending. However, in the summer of 2024, the number of tourists visiting our state
dipped by 9%, underscoring the need for adaptable labor policies to maintain the quality of service that visitors expect and to sustain the economic vitality of these sectors.
Extending working hours for minors under 16 provides several benefits, including alleviating staffing shortages, particularly during peak seasons, and offering greater and valuable work experience.
Comparatively, school sports and extracurricular activities can often have time commitments that extend beyond current work limits. Students participating in evening games, practices, or events frequently stay at school past the hour they would be allowed to work. This bill provides a fair balance, ensuring that

young people can have similar flexibility when choosing to gain work experience, just as they do when
participating in school-related activities.

We acknowledge the importance of balancing work opportunities with the well-being and academic
commitments of minors. The proposed extension maintains reasonable limits, ensuring that young workers are not overextended and can continue to prioritize their education.

For these reasons, we urge you to support LD 618. Thank you for your time and consideration. I would be

happy to answer any questions.

TESTIMONY NEITHER FOR NOR AGAINST
L.D. 618
AN ACT TO ALLOW MINORS UNDER 16 YEARS OF AGE TO WORK UNTIL 9 P.M. DURING THE SCHOOL YEAR AND UNTIL 10 P.M. DURING SUMMER VACATION
March 18, 2025
Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and members of the Labor Committee, I am Steven Bailey, the executive director of Maine School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School Boards Association and the Maine School Superintendents Association neither for nor against L.D. 618, which proposes extending the permissible work hours for minors under 16 years of age. We would like to offer some considerations regarding the impact of student employment, emphasizing that the ultimate decision on a student's work schedule should be determined by the parent or guardian.
All student's circumstances are unique, and parents or guardians are best positioned to determine what balance of work and school is appropriate for their child. While employment can teach critical life skills and financial literacy, it is critical that students maintain their academic commitments and personal well-being.
Our concerns about extending work hours are that late work hours may lead to fatigue, reducing focus and performance in school. Students will need to balance school, extracurricular activities, and work, which will be stressful, impacting their well-being. Working additional hours may reduce opportunities for family interaction, extracurricular engagement, and social development.
Extending work hours may provide some benefits to students, but it is essential to ensure that their academic success and personal development remain a priority. We ask the committee to consider safeguards that support student well-being and to affirm that the decision on a student's work schedule ultimately rests with their parent or guardian.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Steven W. Bailey
MSBA Executive Director

Eileen E. King
MSSA Executive Director
